tweets.title: One of the challenges for training Theory of Mind models is the lack of ground-truth mental state annotations. How can we address this? It turns out that you do
tweets.body:
One of the challenges for training Theory of Mind models is the lack of ground-truth mental state annotations. How can we address this? It turns out that you don't need any annotations! Introducing MindZero, a self-supervised RL approach for training LLMs to internalize Bayesian inverse planning with ZERO annotations, accepted to #ICML2026.

Key idea: Bayesian inverse planning provides self-supervised reward for training an LLM; after training, LLM generates amortized inferences end-to-end. This is a significant step toward scaling Bayesian inverse planning style Theory of Mind reasoning. Check out @ShunchiZhang's thread for details 👇

tweets.title: To plan effectively in an unseen 3D world, embodied agents need to form and update beliefs of the 3D world. In our recent work, @yifanyin_11 proposed 3D-Belief,
tweets.body:
To plan effectively in an unseen 3D world, embodied agents need to form and update beliefs of the 3D world. In our recent work, @yifanyin_11 proposed 3D-Belief, a generative 3D world model that continuously updates  scene memory AND 3D imagination of unseen space as an agent explores a new environment. We show great results of improved imagination quality 🖼️, spatial reasoning 🌎, and closed-loop planning 🤖 with 3D-Belief. This work presents a new way to think about what kinds of world modeling are necessary for embodied reasoning and planning under partial observability, particularly in unseen environments. 

See the thread below for more details 👇

tweets.title: Users’ interactions with LLMs are driven by their latent thoughts 🧠, such as how they react to LLM responses and why they send follow-up requests. In our recent
tweets.body:
Users’ interactions with LLMs are driven by their latent thoughts 🧠, such as how they react to LLM responses and why they send follow-up requests. In our recent work with @GoogleResearch, we collected ThoughtTrace, a large-scale dataset of user thoughts during multi-turn human-AI interactions. We found that these self-reported thoughts (1) reveal useful information for user behavior modeling and (2) provide learning signals for model alignment that are otherwise unavailable from just the conversations.

Check out the following thread from @chuanyang_jin👇

tweets.body: Real-world, open-ended agents need to continually acquire knowledge and skills after deployment. In our recent work, we introduce AgentOdyssey, a game generator that procedurally creates long-horizon text games for evaluating test-time continual learning agents. This presents a new challenge for LLM agents and continual learning where learning and testing happen at the same time over a long horizon. See @zheyuanzhang99's thread for details.

tweets.title:
Coordinating paths among multiple agents remains extremely challenging, especially in tight spaces. This includes:
🤝 human–robot coordination
🤖 multi-robot coll
tweets.body:
Coordinating paths among multiple agents remains extremely challenging, especially in tight spaces. This includes:
🤝 human–robot coordination
🤖 multi-robot collaboration

Communication helps, but we still lack generalizable models that ground language in multi-agent path planning for open-ended environments.

In a new work led by two amazing undergrads in our lab, Haojun Shi and @suyu_ye, we introduce:

🧩 Code as Path Editor (CaPE), a safe, interpretable multimodal framework for multi-agent path coordination.

Key idea:
Instead of asking a model to generate robot trajectories directly, CaPE trains a small VLM to act as a path editor.
1️⃣ A conventional planner proposes paths
2️⃣ The VLM converts language + current state into structured path edits
3️⃣ Edits are verified against safety constraints before execution

This makes CaPE:
✅ Safe (constraint-verified)
🔍 Interpretable (explicit path edits)
🔌 Plug-and-play (works with existing planners)

The result: strong generalization across diverse settings with zero finetuning, including
1) human-robot teaming in household tasks
2) human-robot joint object carrying
3) multi-robot coordination

tweets.body: AutoToM can also discover relevant history in the context (e.g., an agent’s past behavior), whether prior works often assume all history is relevant. Such ability is crucial in AutoToM’s success in ToM reasoning given long context while reducing computational cost.

tweets.title: Conventional Bayesian inverse planning assumes a given model (e.g., MDP, POMDP, I-POMDP) to interpret agent behavior in a specific domain. AutoToM fully automat
tweets.body: Conventional Bayesian inverse planning assumes a given model (e.g., MDP, POMDP, I-POMDP) to interpret agent behavior in a specific domain. AutoToM fully automates this process, adapting Bayesian inverse planning to open-ended scenarios without any domain knowledge.
